hook.line: Every kitchen has a drawer of things nobody uses. When you want to say something is truly useless, *no sirve para nada* does it in four words.
hook.es: Ese aparato no sirve para nada, es un cacharro.
hook.en: That gadget is no use at all; it's a piece of junk.

rule:
To say something is useless, use *no servir para nada* (the everyday choice in Latin America) or *no valer para nada*. Literally: "it does not serve for anything".

Spanish happily uses two negatives: *no* before the verb and *nada* after it. English would not.
The verb agrees with the thing: *sirve, sirven*; *vale, valen*.
To ask: *¿Sirve para algo?*
Two useful nouns: *un cacharro* is a junk gadget, and *un estorbo* is something in the way. Both are masculine.
smallPrint: Teachers call this a double negative: in Spanish it is the normal way, not a mistake.

pitfalls.right: Ese aparato no sirve para nada.
pitfalls.why: Almost. English "no use at all" hides the little word; Spanish needs *para*.

pitfalls.wrong: Esos aparatos no sirve para nada.
pitfalls.right: Esos aparatos no sirven para nada.
pitfalls.why: Almost. The verb agrees with the thing, and there are several.
Almost. *Estorbo* is masculine, even when the table is feminine.

personal: Think of something at home you never use. Say it: *No sirve para nada.*
